name: Festuca
look_here_first: FIRST: compare the ROOTED plant and actual whole branching head. SIXWEEKS FESCUE F. octoflora (= Vulpia octoflora) is usually a very small cool-season ANNUAL on dry rocky/open ground with compact one-sided awned panicles. TEXAS FESCUE F. versuta is a PERENNIAL wooded-calcareous bunch with a more open, branched flowering head. In this visual learner a CC-licensed actual F. octoflora whole plant/spikelet appears alongside a PUBLIC DOMAIN 1906 drawing labeled F. johnsoni, an older synonym concept of F. versuta. The drawing is not a photographed plant and the current F. versuta real source photo shows loose fragments. Do not force species identity without an actual rooted base and attached spikelet.

recognition.where_to_look_first: START AT THE WHOLE ROOTED PLANT: SIXWEEKS FESTUCA OCTOFLORA (also Vulpia octoflora) is a narrow-awned SHORT-LIVED ANNUAL; F. VERSUTA / TEXAS FESCUE is a PERSISTENT PERENNIAL. Look for narrow leaves, true small membranous ligule, awned multiflowered spikelets and branch arrangement. Do not diagnose Texas fescue from the current image of loose dry seeds/bracts alone.

comparison_lesson.title: Festuca two-species field comparison
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: ANNUAL tiny upright awned SIXWEEKS vs PERENNIAL Texas fescue. Rooted crown + intact mature panicle mandatory.
quick_split: SIXWEEKS FESCUE = SMALL ANNUAL grass with very NARROW tight upright awned panicles and threadlike blades, frequently drying in late spring. Measure multi-flowered spikelet (~5–10 mm excluding awns) and tiny 0.5 mm ligule, and look for a shallow short-lived fibrous root instead of perennial crown. Also called Vulpia octoflora in many regional floras—same species, not another card.

TEXAS FESCUE = native eastern/southcentral North American PERENNIAL; in the field look for a persistent tuft/crown and branching fescue panicle, then inspect mature spikelets and leaf collar. CAUTION: our archived photo shows loose narrow bracts/grass fragments on a palm, NOT a whole plant, intact panicle, or a secure visible species-diagnostic feature. Do not label each loose fragment a seed without dissection.
comparison_lesson.guardrail: Taxon synonym Vulpia octoflora is the same installed Festuca octoflora concept, not a new species admission. Texas fescue specific county occurrence not audited.

field_traits: Native North American cool-season ANNUAL, often only ~8–40 cm tall and short-lived.
Very fine leaves commonly 1–2 mm wide, often folded or rolled.
Narrow erect panicle, often 3–16 cm long with short appressed branches.
Spikelets usually ~5–10 mm with several (5–13) small florets, each fertile lemma awned.
True ligule very short (~0.5 mm); mature awn/glume length variable across varieties and sources.
Synonym Vulpia octoflora (Walter) Rydb. in many references; no duplicate species admission.
comparisons.how_to_split: Festuca versuta (Texas fescue) is a perennial rather than a 6-weeks spring annual, with a more open branching flowering panicle in mature plants and a persistent base. The existing F. versuta image is loose seed/lemma material, so it does not prove panicle or perennial habit. For other Vulpia spp., dissect unequal glumes and measure lemma and awn instead of using dried color.

field_traits: North American native perennial; exact Hays County occurrence remains unreviewed.
Grass identification should be based on intact plant and spikelets, not scattered seed material.
Perennial crown and taller flowering culms versus small sixweeks annual.
Open to somewhat nodding panicle with multi-flowered fescue spikelets (must verify with intact source-identified individual).
Leaf sheath ligule and any awns require scale macro; current photo insufficient.
comparisons.how_to_split: F. octoflora / Vulpia octoflora is a small short-lived annual with very thin leaves and narrow awned upright panicle. F. versuta is a perennial and may show a more branching panicle and an enduring crown; verify this in a fresh whole-plant image because current loose-bract photo cannot separate them reliably. Also compare Festuca subverticillata/nutans concepts with a regional taxonomic key.

items.label: SIXWEEKS FESCUE — intact annual at Utah rock ledge
items.image_role: Matt Lavin's living Vulpia octoflora flowering plant in Zion, Utah. Small clump with actual attached slender awned flowering panicles, no uprooted roots visible.
items.caption: The small upright grass grows from one low base on dry rock/sand. Slender leaves and a number of narrow, mostly erect flowering branches rise above the base. It shows a single-season SIZE AND HABIT candidate; this photo alone cannot prove lifespan or ligule size.
items.why_it_matters: Our original archived sixweeks image lacked a whole living plant; this shows its compact growing form.

items.label: TEXAS FESCUE — HISTORIC 1906 Festuca johnsoni anatomical plate
items.image_role: HISTORIC BOTANICAL ILLUSTRATION, NOT A PHOTOGRAPH. The 1906 Smithsonian / U.S. National Herbarium plate says 'Festuca johnsoni Vasey', corresponding to Festuca nutans var. johnsonii Vasey / F. johnsonii (Vasey) Piper synonym complex under accepted F. versuta. Contains a rooted/tillered plant, a loose panicle on branch tips, exaggerated detached spikelet, and enlarged bract drawings.
items.caption: Old plate illustrates a thin flowering culm rising from a tufted base, long narrow foliage, an airy branching panicle and separate enlarged spikelet/blade-anatomy drawings. Useful for HOW to recognize reproductive organization but not an exact measured present-day Texas fescue voucher, a live color photo, or proof of all microstructures.
items.why_it_matters: Provides a real historical taxonomic illustration of a synonymous name where the one current Texas-fescue source image shows only loose fragments. Shows field architecture without manufacturing a plant photograph.

items.image_role: Matt Lavin's macro of packed multi-flowered Vulpia octoflora spikelets; distinct pale projecting awns and a narrow crowded one-sided panicle.
